## What this page covers

This page tells the short story of how the RM 8.5 forecast model got to
where it is. There are three steps:

1. We started with neural network scripts that Spencer shared with us.
2. We tried a basic random forest model. It looked good on past years, but
   it ran too cool during the very warm summer of 2026.
3. We switched to a model that predicts the **change** from today's
   temperature, instead of the temperature itself. That fixed most of the
   problem.

The model forecasts the **7DADM** at Whychus Creek RM 8.5, one to seven days
ahead. The 7DADM is the average of the last seven daily high water
temperatures. We compare the forecast to the 20 °C limit in the Habitat
Conservation Plan (HCP).

This is where the model stands for now, not a final answer. We may keep
exploring.

## 1. Where we started: Spencer's neural network scripts

Spencer Sawaske shared scripts (2023) that he used to forecast stream
temperature on the Middle Fork John Day. They are saved in
`data-raw/scripts_from_spencer/`.

The scripts use a **neural network**, a kind of model that learns patterns
from past data. It was given a short list of inputs:

* stream flow
* the day of the year
* the day's highest and lowest air temperature
* yesterday's flow and yesterday's air temperatures

One version also used yesterday's water temperature. A short readme explains
the process in three steps: try different model settings, check how well
each one does, then rebuild the best one. We kept that process.

Two ideas from these scripts are still in our model today:

* **Day of the year**, so the model knows what season it is.
* **The water temperature already measured at the site**, because tomorrow's
  temperature is a lot like today's.

Before using the method on a new creek, we made sure it worked the same way
in R. `mfjd-ann-in-R.R` repeats Spencer's workflow in R using the same
inputs.

## 2. A basic random forest, and where it fell short

### Choosing a random forest

We tried Spencer's approach at RM 8.5 (`rm85-ann.Rmd`). We used our own
inputs: Camp Polk flow and water temperature, and National Weather Service
air temperature and cloud cover. We also tried a **random forest** on the
same inputs. A random forest is many simple decision trees whose answers are
averaged together.

The two models did about the same. We don't report the exact scores,
because those early tests were set up in a way that made the scores
unreliable.

Since accuracy didn't separate them, we picked the random forest for
practical reasons:

* It doesn't need the inputs rescaled or a lot of settings tuned.
* It shows which inputs mattered most. That is important for a forecast that
  helps inform regulatory decisions.
* It is easier to retrain and to run every day.

### What went wrong in summer 2026

This first version predicted the water temperature itself. When we tested it
on summer 2026, it ran **too cool**, and the problem was worst on the warm
days that matter most:

* On average it was too cool by 0.9 °C at one day ahead, growing to 1.9 °C
  at seven days ahead.
* On days that were 20 °C or warmer, it was too cool by about 1.0 °C on
  average.
* At seven days ahead it was no better than simply guessing that the 7DADM
  would stay the same as today (an error of 2.01 °C compared with 2.05 °C).

Summer 2026 was unusually warm. It was warmer than every earlier summer we
have data for:

```{r stationarity, echo = FALSE}
season <- rm_8_5_historical |>
  filter(statistic == "7DADM", !is.na(temperature)) |>
  mutate(date = as.Date(date)) |>
  arrange(date) |>
  filter(lubridate::month(date) %in% 5:10) |>
  mutate(delta7 = if_else(as.numeric(date - lag(date, 7)) == 7,
                          temperature - lag(temperature, 7), NA_real_))

by_year <- season |>
  group_by(year = lubridate::year(date)) |>
  summarise(level_mean = mean(temperature),
            delta_sd   = sd(delta7, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(!is.na(delta_sd))

# 2026 comes from the new RM 8.5 logger, which is not part of the packaged
# historical record, so these two values are added by hand.
by_year_2026 <- tibble(year = 2026, level_mean = 21.3, delta_sd = 1.89)

bind_rows(by_year, by_year_2026) |>
  transmute(Summer = as.character(year),
            `Average 7DADM (°C)` = level_mean,
            `Typical weekly change (°C)` = delta_sd) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1,
               caption = paste("Average 7DADM for each May-October season, and",
                               "how much the 7DADM typically changes over a",
                               "week (the standard deviation of 7-day",
                               "changes). There is no RM 8.5 data for 2023."))
```

Earlier summers averaged between
`r round(min(by_year$level_mean), 1)` and `r round(max(by_year$level_mean), 1)` °C.
Summer 2026 averaged 21.3 °C, which is about 4.6 °C above a typical summer.

### Why it missed

We first wondered whether the model had simply never seen water this warm.
That turned out not to be the whole story. About a third of the days in the
training data were 20 °C or warmer, and the hottest day the model predicted
was within 1 °C of the hottest day actually observed.

We did find two causes:

* **The weather forecasts didn't match.** The model learned from archived
  weather forecasts, but when it runs for real it gets the live National
  Weather Service forecast. They aren't the same, and the small differences
  add up, especially for forecasts further ahead.
* **The creek changed around 2022.** A model built on the early years
  (2011-2015) predicted RM 8.5 about 2 °C too cool in 2022, 2024 and 2025,
  given the same Camp Polk temperatures. The gap stays about the same size
  each year instead of slowly growing, which points to a one-time shift, not
  gradual drift.

A model that predicts the temperature itself carries both of these errors
straight into its forecast. It also has a built-in limit: a random forest
can never predict a value outside the range it saw while learning. In a
summer as unusual as 2026, that limit matters.

## 3. Switching to a "change from today" model

### The idea

Instead of predicting the temperature, the model predicts **how much the
temperature will change** from today. We then add that change to the 7DADM
the RM 8.5 logger measured today:

> forecast = today's 7DADM + predicted change

For example, if the 7DADM is 22 °C today and the model predicts a rise of
1.5 °C, the forecast is 23.5 °C.

### Why it works better

**1. It starts from a real measurement.** The starting point is what the
logger actually measured, not something the model has to rebuild from
weather forecasts and Camp Polk. A weather forecast that is a bit off can
nudge the predicted change, but it can't throw off the starting point.

**2. Changes stay in the usual range, even in an unusual year.** Summer 2026
was far warmer than any other summer, but the week-to-week changes were
about the normal size (see the table above). A random forest struggles
outside the range it learned from. The change stays inside that range, so
the forest stays in familiar territory.

**3. The model can focus on what is uncertain.** A lot of what makes
temperature vary is just the seasons: warm in summer, cool in winter. When
the model predicts the temperature itself, it has to work that out again.
When it starts from today's temperature, the season is already built in. All
of the model's effort goes to the part we don't know: how the temperature
will move.

### How it did

On the summer 2026 test, the change-from-today version had an average error
of about 0.3 °C at one day ahead and about 1.0 °C at seven days ahead. On
days that were 20 °C or warmer, the cool bias dropped to under 0.5 °C, where
it had been as much as 1.8 °C. It also beat the guess "tomorrow will look
like today" at every forecast length. Of everything we tested, this change
made the biggest difference.

### Things to keep in mind

* **It needs a current RM 8.5 reading every day.** If the sensor is off, the
  forecast will be off by the same amount. We couldn't have used this
  approach before the RM 8.5 logger was installed.
* **It works because temperature carries over from one day to the next.**
  That helps less the further ahead we forecast. We haven't found the point
  where it stops helping.
* **It isn't a new trick.** Predicting the change instead of the level is a
  common technique in forecasting. Time-series analysts call it
  *differencing*.
